subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not about to accuse you of becoming lazy or indifferent.
Just as the oil in the ground and the resources belong to the provinces, the resources of the Atlantic area belong to the Atlantic provinces. As long as we continue with ad hoc solutions to the problems and ignore the development of the opportunity that lies before us, the question of the provinces again assuming authority over the fisheries will be debated.
The minister would be the first to admit that there are many areas in which he wishes he could do more. Most fishermen that I know have a fair amount of respect for the minister. In some instances they have come to rely on his judgment, to respect his caution and to accept his word about methods of resolving their problems. I am not going to refer to the minister seeking the leadership of a party somewhere else although he might be an adornment to his province if he did so; but, Mr. Speaker, we must face the fact that the minister might not always be here and in that light his assurances cannot be taken for more than that-just assurances.
The minister will do those things he believes to be important but that is not good enough for the fishery. It is not good enough to say that the schedule of fees will not be usurious but will be applied with care and concern. The people want something more specific and in the absence of an explanation the minister is treading on very dangerous ground. He is assuming a responsibility and authority that the people affected will not accept.

The only provisions in the bill that are new are the schedule of fees and minor changes in three or four areas. For the most part the bill consolidates and brings under one umbrella a lot of practices that are common and acceptable. What cannot be accepted is the assurance that these things will not hurt the fishery. Unless the minister can demonstrate to the fishermen that some of these charges will not be usurious, they will not trust him. Our own view flows from a desire to be open and frank and to tell the fishermen what we would do and how we would do it.
The minister has given himself wide authority and far-reaching powers in this bill. Many people in the fishery are outraged when they see pork barrelling, and an increase in the numbers of wharfingers. They do not like the continuing conflict between the minister and his provincial colleagues. We in this party want a better relationship between the fishery and the search and rescue capability. We also want improved repair and maintenance of wharves and breakwaters. We are told that because we catch only about 2 per cent of the fishery we are only entitled to 2 per cent of the money. Mr. Speaker, how does the minister expect us to do any better unless we are given wharves and harbours so that our young people may be encouraged to go into the fishery?
I asked the minister about dredging the Musquodoboit harbour and he said it could not be done. Mr. Speaker, it has the potential to become one of the finest private small craft harbours on the Atlantic seaboard. The Department of Public Works said they could not do it, but a local firm claimed they could do it in half a day. They said the job was too small for them, however. The Department of Public Works, on the other hand, thought the job was too big for them to tackle. There was only a handful of fishermen there, Mr. Speaker. It was not only the fishermen 1 asked about, but also the capacity of Musquodoboit harbour to handle boats and become a location for a series of marinas which would encourage private sailing and private use by Americans and people from other parts of Atlantic Canada as they traversed the south and east coasts of Nova Scotia.
We need the co-operation and the understanding of the treasury benches and the government that the fisheries require substantially higher funding. We need to end the disparate attitude which accompanies so much of the decision-making process within government in areas such as the fishery. We need to develop both our inshore and offshore fisheries. We do not need the hocus-pocus that the minister must sometimes go through in order to hide from our Atlantic fishermen the difficulty he has in convincing his colleagues in government that there is anything worth while in the fishing industry.
As a matter of fact, the only other member of the entire cabinet whom 1 have heard refer to the fishery in the last two or three years has been the Secretary of State of External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson). No other minister, including the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald), who comes from a great fishing riding, has bothered to mention it at all.



February 6, 1978

We need a better spirit amongst the people and the generation of enthusiasm. We need more than FLIP and LIP programs to develop our fishery.
The licence fees should be increased and the money used to improve the Loran and Decca systems. I do not mind soaking the foreigners who are off our coasts. For 10 or 15 years they have had a free ride on the backs of those navigational systems. Take the money from them. Do not put it into general revenue unless it is absolutely certain that every nickel is returned to the fishermen by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). Every cent that is raised belongs to the fishermen of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. That money should be poured back into the development of their own resource.
That is the reason for my suggestion of the return of authority and control over the fishery to the provinces. I say return because this parliament, not this chamber precisely, took it away from the provinces in the beginning. The provinces can get it back. We must demonstrate a willingness to help the fishermen develop their own resources and their own livelihood to levels that are acceptable and most important, to bring it to levels that will encourage young people to return to the fishery. I do not blame the provinces for saying they wished they had more control.
If the principle of equalization is to have any meaning over the next 20 to 30 years, it will have to find justification, rationalization and a changed attitude on the part of this government toward the fishermen. But I think the minister has been abandoned. There has been such a preoccupation in the last ten years with matters other than those which are basic to our way of life that our basic primary resources have suffered. I repeat, we do not need ad hoc programs; we need programs that flow from reality. We need more money. We need to open up our ports. We need to create jobs in the shipyards. These things have to be done. Trust must be re-established between the minister and the fishermen with respect to the scheduling of fees. What will be the amount of the fees and how great will the impact be on the fishermen? These are the essentials. We must seize the opportunity, but with caution, and ensure that this economic generator is developed in the best way possible for the advancement of people on the east and west coasts as well as the advancement of our very rich nation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to say a few words about Bill C-2. I am not given to praising people too highly because I am always afraid it might go to their heads. But the fact remains that in all sincerity I must say to the minister that 1 am under the impression that in the present circumstances he put in a lot of heart and time to try and bring a little help and relief first to fishermen and then to vacationers, those who have pleasure boats.
Personally, I am not jealous that others have marinas and fishing harbours. I think, and the minister is certainly aware of this, that Quebec is clearly underprivileged when it comes to recreational and fishing harbours for small and medium size boats when you consider that certain provinces have over 2,000
Fishing and Recreational Harbours recreational harbours and there are only some 30 of them in Quebec at most, I believe.
This brings me naturally to talk about the Lower St. Lawrence area that I represent, namely Rimouski. I do not know whether the minister knows the Rimouski area but 1 think he knows it quite well. He is no doubt aware that Rimouski is a rather strategic area for pleasure boats. Indeed, judging from last year's business figures, the port of Rimouski is the second most important after, I think, Sept-Iles.
There are also many social clubs, sporting clubs and many owners of pleasure crafts in Rimouski. There are also a dozen fishermen living mostly off fishing there. Unfortunately they have no place to moor or tie up their craft. Of course there is the port of Rimouski but it is exposed in bad weather and there is difficulty in keeping the boats secure. Those fishermen fishing for cod, red fish or other species of fish in the gulf estuary would be quite happy naturally, even if they had to pay reasonable mooring fees to have a place to tie up their boats, land their catches and occasionally be able to make a few minor repairs.
Mr. Speaker, nor should we forget either pleasure craft owners who would be quite willing to pay mooring fees inasmuch as these fees are reasonable and that adequate services are available. As the minister knows, the city of Rimouski is some 350 miles downstream from Montreal and close to 200 miles from Quebec city in the quadrangle formed by Riviere-du-Loup, Saguenay, Matane and Baie-Comeau. The river width in these places can reach 50 miles. Sometimes the sea can be rather rough especially when there are strong winds which are called "nordet" in that area, or northeast winds if you want. I think it is more or less comparable with prevailing conditions in the Chaleur Bay so there is a lot of danger when we do not have any safe place to moor our boats.
The city of Rimouski has some 30 to 40 small boat owners. The city also boasts a marine school and a research centre sponsored by the University of Quebec. In addition, Rimouski has a university which can provide any courses related to fisheries and navigation.
Mr. Speaker, it is for all these reasons that I am asking the minister to provide us with adequate services because Rimouski and the areas of Bic, Sainte-Flavie and Sainte-Luce have been deprived of such services for too long. As I said earlier, we are not very well known, but I think that it would be high time now, in the spring of 1978, to build a marina suited to and worthy of the largest city in the lower St. Lawrence region. Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay this debate any longer and I am urging the minister in the name of the people of Rimouski to put an end to the delays which the whole population of the lower St. Lawrence has been enduring regarding the building of a marina in Rimouski and at the same time provide improvements to the existing services for the dozens of fishermen in that area. I am also asking the minister if the Canada-Quebec agreements have now been

signed and if he will indicate to me in his answer if he can really grant my request.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the first occasion I have had to speak on either Bill C-2 or its predecessor which was introduced for second reading and debate on December 10, 1976. I reread the speech made by the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) on that occasion. I listened with real interest to the debate that took place on Bill C-2.
1 do not want to delay the House for too long; however, there are a few matters on which I would like to comment as well as a few points with regard to the measure as it affects the province of British Columbia. The legislative provisions deal with two particular interests of our society in general. Both of these are of great importance to British Columbia. I refer to the fishing industry and also the recreation and tourist industry.
In introducing this bill, the minister stated, as recorded at page 2413 of Hansard:
This act will provide the necessary legislative authority to develop and administer commercial fishing and recreational harbours in Canada in order to meet the changing requirements of the fisheries and the growing needs of sports fishing and recreational boating.
It is well known that the fishing industry is of paramount interest to the province of British Columbia. Because of the extent of that industry, it is vital to the maintenance of a healthy economy as well.
With regard to the commercial fishery, direct employment in the British Columbia fishing industry is about 100,000 persons. The direct export value of the product is about $250 million per year. The level of investment in the fishing fleet, equipment, plant and machinery is approximately $1 billion. Therefore, we see that this is not a small sector of the British Columbia economic picture or just a small part of the national picture. It is of substantial concern and interest.
The question may be asked why I, living somewhat more distant from the coast than some of my colleagues, would have an interest in the fisheries. I would point out that consideration must be given to the fact that the Fraser fishery is the mainstay of the British Columbia fishing industry. I have the honour to represent part of the Fraser river area. It is questionable whether the industry could remain viable without the fishery of the Fraser river.
The British Columbia fishing industry is one of a very few industries in Canada which is entirely vertically integrated, responsible for harvesting, processing and marketing of renewable natural resources in the finished form. The Pacific Trailers' Association points out it is also labour intensive and highly export oriented. What makes the industry unique is its relative independence from any direct support or subsidy by public funds. It does not require elaborate tariff and non-tariff protection for its existence. The association presentation also points out that the industry accounts for some $250 million
[Mr. Allard.)
annual in direct exports. Therefore, we can see that fisheries is an important industry in the province of British Columbia.
In our consideration of this industry, we ought to give a little more attention to the west coast fishery. Many times we find that we are left out of the discussion and debate. Since coming here some years ago, I have found that in many areas of activity British Columbia seems just a little bit too far away to be brought into the usual area of concern, discussion and debate.
Reference was made to the sports fishery. Statistics show that the sports fishery in Canada employs over 100,000 individuals and generates about $1 billion for the economy. The present value of sports fishing boats in Canada is approximately $2 billion. At one point in the minister's presentation he mentioned that a great proportion of this activity would be in the province of British Columbia. In participating in this debate, I want again to emphasize the importance of the fishing industry. The bill before us certainly does concern itself with this industry.
British Columbia's extensive coastline and relatively small number of wharves and facilities presents the possibility of a greater, healthier, and more economic industry if proper steps are taken, not only to catch up with present requirements, but to provide future growth opportunities.
Sometimes we are content just to look at the situation as it exists at present. We try to adapt our proposals, legislation and programs to meet the situation as it is at the moment. There must be vision in the matter of providing facilities. We have to look far beyond the present. If we are to have the growth that we desire, we must plan for the future.
I wish to make a few comments with regard to recreation. It is equally well known that our tourist and recreational aspects make British Columbia the land of recreation for Canadians. In spite of what the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling) said, we still believe that British Columbia is Canada's evergreen playground. It is true there are times when the green is covered by a white substance, but that only adds to the beauty and attractiveness of the area.
Recreation is not only a local effort. It is tied in with tourism which has become one of our principal industries. Some people might suggest that in the face of the tremendous problems confronting Canada the government should concentrate only on areas which are a major source of concern and that in the field of recreation the people directly concerned should provide whatever is required.
The recreational aspect of the bill has a wider application than just meeting the needs and desires of local people in the community. It has a bearing upon the tourist industry. If facilities are not available we shall not be able to attract tourists to our country, and to British Columbia in particular. This is a matter of major concern. There has been a great deal of debate about the imbalance of the tourist account and it seems to me this is an area which requires a good deal of attention.


****HnmHraimi
February 6, 1978

Urbanization has resulted in an effort on the part of a growing number of people to find relaxation and renew their physical and mental health in less populated areas. In British Columbia, roads have reached the point of such congestion- and this is true of other regions-that people hesitate to go out on them on holiday weekends. Nevertheless, more people than ever are finding their way to the waterways, lakes and camping areas and it is essential to provide wharves, marinas and ramps to meet their needs. Accordingly, I believe the inclusion of recreational facilities as one of the benefits of this bill is understandable. My own province would benefit not only directly but indirectly through the tourist industry. We should be looking not only at the present but to the requirements of future development.
There are several features in the bill which are causing apprehension and I should like to refer to some of them. They have already been dealt with to some extent, perhaps to a considerable extent, by my hon. friends, but I should like to associate myself with what they have said because they have been expressing the concern of a great many people across the country.
Reference has been made to the fee structure. The uncertainty with respect to this feature of the bill is a major problem. I realize that in the debate in which the minister took part he pointed out, as recorded at page 2414, that he did not intend to take any precipitate action, that nothing was contemplated at the present time but that at some time in the future consideration would have to be given to the imposition of a fee schedule so as to provide income for the various programs contemplated by the department.
This is not a sufficient assurance. It has been pointed out on many occasions that no matter how well intentioned the minister of the day might be no one knows when the situation will change. Some new minister might come along and say: "This is a matter which should have been taken care of during the debates on Bill C-2; we shall impose a fee structure without further delay." This is what is bothering those in the industry. I believe the minister should be more specific in outlining his intentions for the future as far as a fee structure is concerned.
He has indicated there will be a varying set of fees; in other words, that fees will not be the same across the country. This type of thinking is all too prevalent in the government's planning. We see it in tariffs, in transportation and in other directions. It is a source of real resentment among the people of British Columbia who feel they are treated differently from people in other parts of the nation. It is irksome. People are wondering when the government will come to the conclusion that British Columbia is an integral part of the nation. If national unity is to be maintained the government will have to look upon British Columbia as being an essential part of Canada and act accordingly.
I notice that as reported on page 2414 the minister said:
The nucleus of the proposal we will bring to the fishermen is how we can best devise a fee system which will not only recognize market demand and relate to the level and quality of services provided but which will recognize regional
Fishing and Recreational Harbours differences. Obviously this means we are not going to be illogical enough, particularly in the case of east coast fishermen, to subsidize on the one hand and take it back through an unreasonable fee structure on the other.
We have no objection to consideration being given to the problems facing the fisheries on the east coast, but I believe if we are going to consider fees on that basis we must also take into account the needs of fishermen on the west coast. Speaking in another debate some time ago I pointed out that the industry in British Columbia was facing almost insuperable obstacles in its fight to maintain markets in the centre of the nation because of subsidy programs, lower wage rates and lower transportation costs in the east. I suggested that, as a measure of justice and equity, some form of compensation ought to be provided. When we come to the imposition of a fee structure, this aspect has to be taken into account as well.
I should like to refer now to a letter, a copy of which was sent to me, having to do with a statement made by the federal Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) to the Vancouver Province. The minister said that while details of the licensing arrangements still have to be worked out he is committed to the principle of a tax to cover some of the cost of salmon enhancement programs. The problem, the minister said, was making sure the cost of an enforcement of the program did not eat up the benefits. There would be some enforcement but it was not desirable to let the administrative produce so much ill will that it had to be changed.
Replying to this statement, the minister of energy, transportation and communications of British Columbia wrote to the minister under date of January 25. 1 wish to quote one or two passages from that letter. He said:
We looked into this matter carefully when 1 was Fisheries Minister and the cost of the scheme was comparable to the revenue produced. And the research or statistical value was just about nil. You don't get a complete record of the number of fishermen involved and you don't get any data on the number of fish caught. So it won't help us to manage the fishery either.
This is the opinion of one who was minister of fisheries here in Ottawa and who is now minister of energy, transportation and communications in British Columbia. He pointed out that these matters were considered, but that it was not worth the work, the time nor the animosity which would be stirred up because the revenue produced would be spent on operating the program. Also he pointed out the problem in regard to the fee structure. The closing paragraph of his letter reads as follows:
So 1 again urge you to treat us the same way that sports fishermen are treated in other saltwater areas of Canada. Keep the federal bureaucracy to a minimum and we'll all be better off as a result.
The minister should take cognizance of this particular reference which was made by one of his former colleagues. Perhaps there is some question as to the application of fees, but the real thrust of this letter is the unequal application of the program on the west coast as compared to elsewhere.
The degree of consultation was a matter brought to the attention of the minister. The government is not noted for its willingness to engage in productive consultation. Rather, confrontation has been the order of the day. It is not necessary for

February 6, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours me to refer to the various measures brought before the House, nor is it necessary to refer to government attitudes which have been discussed before. Rather than engaging in consultation, the government partakes in a brief discussion and then proceeds. It says, "Take it or leave it. This is the way it will be, regardless of what you think". The minister should enter into real consultation with the provinces and those concerned in order to arrive at something which is acceptable and equitable, that will apply in an equitable fashion to those engaged in similar industries.
The matter of ministerial power has been mentioned by a number of hon. members. I will not refer to this at any length, except to say that this particular measure provides the minister with the authority to move out and lease facilities to any person. He can designate those who will be the enforcement officers. It does not stipulate their qualifications or anything else about them. It provides the minister with the ability to make decisions unilaterally without respect to any other considerations, which is unacceptable and could cause a great deal of harm to the minister because of the possibility of patronage.
I want to associate myself with the concerns which have been expressed by my colleagues in the hope that perhaps our combined efforts will move the minister to respond in a positive way to the reservations and views which have been expressed. If he responds in a positive manner, this bill could be made much more acceptable than it is at the present time.

As soon as the title refers to "certain fishing and recreational harbours in Canada", 1 become somewhat twitchy.

speechtext: They are out poaching.

speechtext:
I doubt that. The people who are out working in those areas are honest and dedicated. If it were not for those beleaguered few, the fishing industry would be in real trouble.
As some of my colleagues have already pointed out, several clauses in this bill tend to make us apprehensive. I should like to refer to clause 5(1) which reads as follows:
The minister may undertake projects for the acquisition, development, construction, improvement or repair of any scheduled harbour or any fishing or recreational harbour to which this act applies.
Perhaps that language is normal, assuming the people out in the fishing areas are extensions of the minister. Too often that is not the case. The decision-making power still rests in Ottawa. While there may be a decentralization, it is a decentralization of administration and not of the decision-making process of the government. Thus, fishermen in the extremities of our country are faced with decisions made in Ottawa which do not properly apply to the regions.
For example, some time ago the minister and his officials decided to upgrade, rebuild or construct a new facility in Steveston Harbour. I am sure the minister is well aware of that project because it is sizeable. In fact, it is a $12 million project. The harbour was designed to accommodate ultimately 1,000 boats. Is that correct? I see the minister is nodding his head. The first phase of that project is designed for 350 boats. No one can argue about that. If it is to be expanded to accommodate 1,000 boats, one must assume the boats will come from far up the Fraser river to use the facilities at Steveston Harbour, unless the majority of the boats are recreational. It would be expecting an awful lot of fishermen to come from far up the Fraser river to use Steveston Harbour. This is an example of the minister deciding which harbour should be developed and developing it to the size he feels is necessary. That is not what the fishermen want. I was talking to them during the Christmas recess. I spent time with them in my office. I went to the harbours that we are talking about. They need facilities on site where their boats and homes are. Rather than one large complex at Steveston, the fishermen require a smaller one there, plus one at Ladner, one at Gunderson and one at New Westminster. I understand there will be a development at Ladner. I will elaborate on that later. Rather than one development for 1,000 boats, why not have four developments for 300 boats each?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext: Basically Steveston Harbour is a winter tie-up.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION AND DEVELOPMENT OF CERTAIN HARBOURS
speechtext:
As much as I hate to admit it, even in December it is winter in British Columbia. I was at the Gunderson slew. There are boats tied up five deep at Gunderson, 15 or 20 miles away from Steveston. They are on land and in dry dock. They are all over the place along the Fraser river. The minister refers to Steveston as mainly a winter tie-up, but does he expect the fishermen to go 15 or 20 miles downstream, into open water and around to Steveston harbour to tie up? To me, that is another example of an Ottawa decision.
February 6, 1978

I am happy to hear that the Ladner harbour is to be the recipient of something in the neighbourhood of $300,000 under FLIP. This really is no skin off the nose of the small harbours department because this is a winter works program, but it is a good thing for the fishermen and I am glad to hear of it.
The minister was in Vancouver on January 26 and spoke to the fishermen there. They in turn brought a number of things to his attention, one, for example, in respect of licensing fees. 1 know some of my colleagues have already brought this to the minister's attention, but there is a great deal of concern out there relative to the expected cost of licence fees. Is the fee to be $2, or $2 a foot? First of all, it is passing strange that we would adopt a fee schedule that has been used for pleasure craft and apply it to fishing operations. Is the fee to be $2 on the west coast and $1 on the east coast? We do not know, but again the feeling is that the very sweeping powers contained in the bill are too great.
I refer particularly to that part of the bill which states that the governor in council may make regulations prescribing schedules naming and delimiting or describing fishing or recreational harbours under the control and administration of the minister, the granting of licences to persons, and so on. Some of these things are logical but the fishermen have a right to know what they are going to have to pay. They certainly have the right to equity in that the fees ought to be the same on the west and east coasts. This is one concern they brought to the minister's attention.
The fishermen feel very strongly that the licence fees they are already paying for fishing ought to be sufficient. They are paying anywhere from $100 or $400 and feel perhaps that ought to be enough to cover the cost of mooring at docks. I know the minister says that the money goes into general revenue and then into the salmon enhancement program. I do not know that the fishermen are convinced this always happens. The fishermen see the amount of money paid into the licensing program and the amount being spent on the salmon enhancement program for British Columbia, but I think they would like to have some concrete evidence that the amount of money going into general revenue does end up for salmon enhancement. The minister shakes his head and I will not suggest what he is thinking because this is a polite society. No doubt he will have something to say about this a little later on, but I am telling the minister this is what the fishermen are concerned about. They are not convinced that the minister is playing ball with them. They wonder if some of that money going into general revenue is not being used in some other way.
There is another clause of this bill that was brought to the attention of the minister, and it is of great concern to me. This is the provision in clause 11 regarding search and seizure. Let me refer to that for a moment. It states in part:
Where an enforcement officer believes on reasonable grounds that a provision of this Act or the regulations is not being complied with, he may
(a) board any vessel or enter any vehicle or premises where or in respect of which he reasonably believes there may be evidence of such non-compliance and make any inspection he deems necessary;-
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
On the surface that seems to be reasonable. I am sure there could well be hanky-panky along the coast. Obviously when you are out in the "boonies" you might be tempted to play hanky-panky with the law, but this seems to be a very broad provision. Perhaps the minister will correct me, but it seems that the search and seizure described is without warrant. Am I right in that regard? There seems to be no need for a warrant on the part of an enforcement officer. Who are the enforcement officers? Are they to be fisheries officials, harbours officials or police officers, or will they be anybody deputized by the minister who will be allowed on any kind of suspicion to go on board a vessel and search, seize and hold properties, as I read the bill, for a specified length of time?
Perhaps the minister will clear these matters up when he responds, but at the present time I am concerned about the kind of powers contained in this bill. When the minister was in Vancouver he said to the fishermen that nothing was final. Those are words quoted to me by the fishermen. He said nothing was final.

speechtext:
The fishermen understood the minister to say that we were approaching report stage on this bill and nothing was final, implying obviously that things could be changed. Yet I have not seen any changes forthcoming. Even if the thing is final we are supposed to trust the minister. 1 think he has been doing a pretty good job as Minister of Fisheries. I do not always agree with him but on the whole I think he is doing a good job. I do not mind trusting him as I do not think he would abuse his powers, nor would he like it if his officials did.
This minister holds this portfolio now, but what are we going to do if, for example, the present Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) were to become the minister of fisheries? Then we would be in trouble. What would be even worse is if the present Minister of State (Environment), the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand), were to become the minister of fisheries. Then we would really be in trouble. As I say, I do not mind trusting this minister, but there are 33 other ministers and if any one of them were to become the next minister of fisheries what new climate would exist?
There is one final matter I should like to introduce to this debate, and this at least transcendentally relates to search and seizure powers. There are a number of recreational craft in my riding and in the neighbouring riding of Burnaby-Richmond-Delta. Since my riding impinges on the 49th parallel and crosses waters of the Pacific Ocean, this means that people

February 6, 1978
Fishing and Recreational Harbours
using their pleasure craft occasionally travel into United States waters. This is bound to happen.
Last week I received a distress call from a party whose father had just moved to White Rock from Winnipeg, bought himself a pleasure craft and gone sailing out in the bay. He drifted into U.S. waters and landed there. He did not even know he had landed on United States soil. A customs officer met him, found out he was a Canadian, and after a little tete-a-tete the father returned to Canada thinking everything was fine. Three months later, after the United States customs office sent their records to the Canadian customs office, this man had a visit from a customs officer and received a fine of $400 for not reporting to Canadian customs. On going into the United States he reported to the customs.
When I got back to my constituency office in Surrey I found a letter from a party from Delta to whom a similar thing had happened. The party was in a boat and another boat carrying some friends had motor trouble. Out in the open water the natural law of the sea is that you help somebody in distress. They drifted into United States waters. When they returned, because of the distress they had experienced they forgot to report to Canadian customs. A few months later when the records came to Canada from United States customs another $400 fine was assessed. I have a Xerox copy of the report made by a man from the mobile inspection section on leaving Canada.
Let me first of all say I agree with the customs and excise people that they ought to enforce this law in a very stringent way. When there are many miles of open water, as is the case along the British Columbia coast, one can imagine what could happen if we did not enforce the law very stringently.
There could be smuggling of dope or liquor, illegal immigration, or any kind of smuggling going on on those open waters if we did not enforce the law stringently. But two things should happen. First, the small harbours branch of the minister's department should be co-operating with the U.S. authorities. There should be a liaison between the Canadian and the U.S. authorities so that when Canadians go to U.S. harbours and dock there and report to the U.S. customs officials, U.S. customs officials are encouraged to tell those Canadian boaters that when they land in Canada they should report to the Canadian authorities. All of the boaters who come back do so in good faith, otherwise they would not even have reported to the U.S. authorities. They are not law breakers. They land there, report and then come back. But if for some reason or another they forget to report, zap, they get a $400 fine. They receive no warning whatsoever, just a $400 fine.
Second, many times they drift into U.S. waters without even knowing it. There are almost no market buoys in U.S. waters in that area. If they land somewhere in the U.S. where there is no customs official, who is to say that they will not be apprehended when they come back to Canadian waters? Although the minister wants to assess licence fees for these people, we are getting scant service when it comes to the

particular area along the forty-ninth parallel in the open waters along the B.C. coast. As I said, while I subscribe to the stringent enforcement of the law, it seems to me that something should be done with regard to other kinds of traffic violations. Many a time if there is a traffic violation on the highways, some kind of warning is given by police officers. So it seems entirely reasonable for the same kind of system to be applied with respect to customs and excise.
I bring these matters to the attention of the minister in the hope that he will get in touch with his colleagues in the cabinet and will do something about these unfortunate people who, in spite of wishing to be law-abiding citizens, unwittingly run afoul of the law and are fined $400 without any kind of warning. I encourage the minister to take this matter in hand and do something for the people who use their pleasure craft and get caught in this way.
I am concerned about these areas in the legislation before us and I hope the minister will answer some of the questions I have raised. If I am wrong, I would be glad to hear him tell me so and have him explain to me what is wrong with the perspective I have of this legislation.

I have just completed a tour of my district, which I started during the Christmas recess and continued in the past two weeks, because I know, having been here for ten years, that at
February 6, 1978

about this time every year damage to fishing gear and to small craft harbours needs to be assessed and I can bring the matter the attention of both the provincial and federal governments. I should like to say, without passing out too many bouquets, that I have had the complete co-operation of the area manager and the provincial government in my investigations and assessment of the situation. My conclusion is that we are forgetting our priorities. What has struck me in particular is the effort being made under the Canada Works program to provide many small craft harbours. Perhaps the minister could check with his officials because this problem has been causing a great deal of frustration. subtopic: RESEARCH-INQUIRY AS TO PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE DEVELOPMENT OF MANUFACTURING SECTOR
RESEARCH-INQUIRY AS TO PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE DEVELOPMENT OF MANUFACTURING SECTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last year Canada's deficit in manufactured goods amounted to more than $10 billion; this year we are looking at a $12 billion deficit. A story in the Financial Post of December 17 last entitled "Think Industry or Forget Jobs" indicates that as a
Adjournment Debate
provider of jobs the manufacturing industry has eroded to the point where today it accounts for only 19 per cent of the nation's work force, as against 25 per cent in 1950. Canadian industry does not have a strong technological base. Without the auto pact, defence production sharing and similar bilateral arrangements with the United States, Canada would have few exports of manufactured goods.
Our lack of technological innovation and the problems of transferring technology from government laboratories to meaningful functions in our manufacturing industries are major problems, but not the only ones. Businessmen also point to excessive controls, high taxes, uncertainty about nationalist sentiment, high costs of production and more advantageous wage rates in other nations with lower living standards.
Examples of Canadian industrial success exist, but they must be built upon and multiplied. To do this, a favourable milieu must be established through the development of coherent national policies aimed at enhancing our industrial base.
In a January 25, 1978 news release Hugh Morris, chairman of the Committee for an Independent Canada, cited the 30 per cent decline in research and development since 1970 as a major contributor both to last year's $12 billion deficit in end-product trade and to the capture of almost one-third of all domestic sales by imported goods. Mr. Morris pointed out that our trade deficit in manufactured goods has grown by almost $9 billion since 1970, of which $7 billion is an imbalance with the United States. Mr. Morris suggests that the latter figure represents a loss of more than 350,000 Canadian jobs over a seven year period.
John Bullock, president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, has underlined the drain of Canadian industry and has pointed to our stale, second-hand technology, and the need for research which can make us world leaders in selected manufacturing areas.
Let us take a look at some of the examples of the emerging problems in our manufacturing sector. The answer to order paper question No. 528 shows that in 1970 imports served 26.2 per cent of the total Canadian market for manufactured goods. In 1973 this percentage had risen to 29.2 per cent, and in 1976 it stood at 29.8 per cent.
The answer to order paper question No. 529 shows that in 1970 84.1 per cent of the Canadian market for computer and office equipment was served by imports, and this figure was 85.9 per cent in 1973 and 87.8 per cent in 1976.
The answer to order paper question No. 531 tells the tragic story of the Canadian market for consumer electronic products served by imports. The figure in 1970 was 33.1 per cent; in 1973 it was 42.2 per cent; and in 1976 it was 59.1 per cent.
The answer to order paper question No. 536 cites one area where we should perhaps enjoy a natural advantage, the field of agricultural machinery. But here again imports have been rising and now control a major portion of our market. In 1969
2598

February 6, 1978
Adjournment Debate
the figure was 76.2 per cent; in 1972 it was 83 per cent; and in 1976 it was 82.6 per cent.
The answer to order paper question No. 522 shows us the estimated gap between the domestic market for secondary manufacturers and domestic production of secondary manufacturers in millions of dollars. In 1977 the production gap was $111 million; in 1973 it was $2,665 million; and in 1976 it rose to $5,009 million.
Order paper question No. 690 shows us that as of March 1977, the latest date for which information is available, only 284 out of 712 companies in the electronics sector were known to be conducting research and development programs. This would account for 78 per cent of all companies in the sector with annual sales over $300,000.
Clearly, research and development is the great multiplier that enables Canadians to maintain and improve their high standard of living by producing goods in our industrial sector for sale in Canada and abroad at competitive prices. There is a clear need for a strategy to stimulate significantly our innovative research and development potential in those industries in which we have the potential for a comparative trade advantage. Our performance to date is not good and is getting worse. I urge the ministry of science and technology to roll up its sleeves and, in concert with the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, launch an industrial strategy to get this nation moving forward again.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Milne (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: RESEARCH-INQUIRY AS TO PROGRAMS TO STIMULATE DEVELOPMENT OF MANUFACTURING SECTOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, let me assure the hon. member that I am as concerned as he that the Canadian manufacturing sector should be strong; and it is a matter of First priority with me that the research and development component of that sector should be a vital catalytic force. I say that representing the minister, as a fairly strong nationalist personally, and as a member of the engineering community which is associated with the research effort in Canada.
The government has three distinct sets of measures to stimulate industrial R and D in Canada. In the first place, there are tax measures. Beginning on April 1, 1977, the government extended the investment tax credit to scientific research and development. This means that both current and capital expenditures on research and development will enjoy a credit ranging from 5 per cent to 10 per cent of qualified expenditures depending on the region in Canada where the research is undertaken.
We estimate that the benefits received by industry from this measure in 1977 is estimated to be in the order of $30 million to $35 million. They will accrue mainly to large and medium size Firms carrying out research in Canada. In addition, it is important to note that, as well as the investment tax credit, an immediate deduction for both capital and current expenditures on scientific research related to the business of the taxpayer is

permitted. This treatment is quite generous since these costs are often not directly related to the earning of current income.
A second measure taken by the government to stimulate research and development in the manufacturing sector is the contracting out policy. For several years, Canadian business has been invited to provide on a competitive basis certain scientific and technological services required in support of new R and D programs. Last year, this policy was extended to ongoing R and D programs as well as related scientiFic activities. Research contracts have increased from $18 million in 1972-73 to approximately $100 million in the last fiscal year.
A third avenue of stimulation for research and development exists in the enterprise development program, established by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce on April 1, 1977. This program provides direct government assistance to industry in the form of loans or grants. The objective of this program is to enhance growth in the manufacturing and processing sectors of the Canadian economy by providing assistance to selected firms in either the area of structural adjustment or innovation, in order to make them viable and internationally competitive. Ministry officials are particularly active in contributing to the decisions of the innovation panel within the enterprise development program.
There are numerous other activities, which 1 have not detailed in this short response, but which are equally as important as some of the above.
The three major thrusts which I have described, namely, tax incentives, the purchase of R and D by the government and direct grants, offer a diversified program of assistance to R and D in Canada, one on which firms, whether they be small, large or medium size, can draw. These programs will be the subject of constant assessment and the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Buchanan) will put forward, as needed, proposals for their extension or modification.

MANPOWER-CANADA WORKS PROGRAM-DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF THIRD PHASE-USE OF SLIPPAGE FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not too often that I get a chance to speak twice within a few minutes! On December 17 I sought information from the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) about the ongoing Canada Works program. I was surprised to learn another change was going to take place. I cannot understand why a good program has to be changed so often. As a result these objectives tend to be forgotten. These objectives were to provide financial aid or assistance to communities, groups or organizations to enable them to use their initiative in providing an economic base or employment opportunities in their area.
The LIP program, Mr. Speaker, started out back in 1971 or 1972. I commended the program for its objectives. After three
February 6, 1978

or four years the monitors, co-ordinators and the people working within the program knew their districts. They knew the people who were sponsoring projects and they knew of the needs of the area. But there was one failing in that it did not provide a program on a five year basis which would allow communities to plan five years ahead. The five year plan would result in an economic base which would provide jobs on a long term basis. I was pleased with the change and I commended the program, as I still do. It can provide what we are seeking.
On December 12, in reply to a question which I posed, the minister indicated that there was to be a further change. This was after I had appealed to people serving on ministerial advisory boards to put the plan on a five-year basis. The program would be in two phases per year, enabling better planning of projects suited to the spring and summer followed by those projects suited for the wintertime. The minister now says that they are going to change the program once more. It will be a one phase program as of next September. Not only did the department change the program, they changed the whole set-up.
After four or five years of the LIP program, I indicated that we had experienced people. When the government implemented the Canada Works program those people experienced on the LIP program were no longer required. They hired new people to learn all over again. We have built up such a bureaucracy in the Canada Works program that it has become confusing to sponsors and to the people who are supposed to help. All those people flying around the country connected with these Canada Works programs have a different interpretation of how it should be run. The employment centres have a different interpretation of the hiring practices, with the result that they are splitting up communities and creating animosity. The member of parliament is caught in the middle.
Perhaps the government would listen to the advice that we are trying to give them. We are always being asked by the other side to tell them about our ideas. I say that the objective of this program is sound. But let us remember what the objectives and aims are. They are to allow every community to define their priorities, and to give themselves an economic base so that not only can they provide short term jobs for the people who need the work but also provide long term jobs, whether it is fisheries, farming or whatever. If the government will only look down the road at this program over the next five to seven years, they will find that every small community in Canada will be able to provide the economic base to give them long term employment. I hope the minister will consider that proposal and review the program as it exists.
I wish I had the time to go into many of the other failings of the program. However, I hope that all members, whether on the government side or on the opposition side of the House, will be able to develop a program which will enable them to obtain the best value for the dollar, to the betterment of this country.

subtopic: MANPOWER-CANADA WORKS PROGRAM-DATE OF ANNOUNCEMENT OF THIRD PHASE-USE OF SLIPPAGE FUNDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 19 the hon. member posed a question to the minister dealing with several of the points he raised tonight. At that time he also asked the minister a question dealing with the slippage funds.
To recap, on December 22, 1977, members were sent a letter informing them how the slippage funds were being distributed. The amount available for distribution was $4,630,000. It was decided that this small amount should be applied to those constituencies which received an allocation lower in phase two than the allocation they received for phase one. The basis for this distribution was that each of these constituencies receive an amount equal to the difference between the constituency allocations for the first and second phases providing that the amount did not exceed either $100,000 or the amount for which there remained acceptable unfunded applications.
To respond more appropriately to the point the hon. member has made this evening, on December 20, 1977, the minister sent a letter informing members of his intention to reorient a significant portion of Canada Works funds for the 1978-79 fiscal year, in order to put more emphasis on the creation of permanent jobs in the private sector. This reorientation involves some $50 million for the economic growth component of Canada Works and the operation of the Canada Works community projects in one year-round phase, rather than two overlapping phases as occurred in 1977-78. Applications for the community projects will be available to the public on April 3, 1978; the application deadline will be June 24, 1978, and projects will commence in September, 1978.
Canada Works is one element of the employment strategy which is to operate over a five-year period ending 1981-82. Each year the government decides the funding distribution to each element in light of the performance of, and changes in, the economy in order that distribution may be directed toward specific situations. So, as the reorientation of the 1978-79 Canada Works program demonstrates, although the employment strategy encompasses a five-year period, it and its elements are nevertheless flexible and subject to yearly assessment and planning.

We had not taken the view the programs of international economic development should be terminated or interrupted because of the political activities of the government of the day.
If that is the case, why is CIDA winding down all their aid programs to Uganda? Angola, another communist-dominated country with Russian and Cuban troops in place, will receive about $2 million for medicine, clothing and roofing materials. I see nothing wrong with the humanitarian aspect of that, but it cuts both ways. If Russia or Cuba are in a position to provide military aid, if they are prepared to move in with troops, arms and guns, surely they can also provide the aid which is essential for reasons of humanity.
Take Ethiopia. CIDA has been sitting on the fence for two or three years trying to decide whether $7.9 million should be spent on a scheme to provide for a water supply in the rural areas. Yet what do we find? We see Ethiopia receiving arms shipments sufficient to overthrow Somalia. We see a heavy Russian presence. We hear warnings from President Sadat that the west should be paying attention to the Russian intrusion in Ethiopia. Yet this government is sending $7.9 million to that country.
A community in my riding, the city of Castlegar, needs $3 million to develop a water supply and I have been trying to get that amount out of the minister for DREE for two years. The stability of the economy of that area, as well as hundreds of jobs, hinges on that $3 million. Besides, I was under the impression that we had an unemployment problem in this country. Surely we should be thinking in terms of Canada first at least in preference to countries which are communist-dominated, communist-oriented, communist-supplied, communist in direction and communist in political persuasion as well as brutal in terms of fellow human beings, countries where humanity is the least consideration.
I say the government is wrong, wrong, wrong in supporting countries of that type and that the money which is wastefully spent in this direction could better be applied to economic programs in this country. If we count up the millions we are

throwing down the tube by making grants to those countries, we would probably find we had enough to provide a small Canada Winter Works program for municipalities. I am not selfish enough to advocate that the money should be channelled into my own riding, but I do submit that much could be accomplished by using the money so wastefully directed to some of these nations to which I have referred.
Finally, I am sure that if I were able to take a poll today of Canadians across this country, members would find they would agree with the position I have taken this evening.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be with the hon. member in this large assembly that we have today. Before making specific comments on the project signed by the government with Ethiopia, I would like to tell the House that after listening to the hon. member saying that this government was wrong, wrong, wrong and that it gave too much assistance to those communist countries, communist in essence, Mr. Speaker, I believe that even though I was a bit young during the McCarthy era in the United States, the speech made by the hon. member could easily be compared with a speech made by McCarthy at that time.
Mr. Speaker, whatever the economic problems of our country and certain communities such as those mentioned by the hon. member or certain villages of the riding I represent, whatever these problems, I believe that a country like Canada cannot forget so easily its duties towards the international community. It is in this spirit that last December the governments of Canada and Ethiopia ratified a protocol of agreement concerning this water resource development project for southern Ethiopia. The hon. member quoted a figure of $7 million, but I must inform him that the figure is not $7 million, but $9 million, and I know he will be even more shocked. It is up to $9 million that Canada has promised to donate to Ethiopia for the professional services and the various types of equipment required for this project. For its part, Ethiopia is willing to contribute a sum equivalent to $3 million in local currency in the form of staff, offices, accommodation, equipment and building materials and other types of required services which are available locally.
Essentially, the long term objective consists in improving the capacity of the Ethiopian government to develop and put to use the water resources of the southern part of the country. As you know, this area is in the Sahel zone which in the last few years has been very seriously affected by droughts which are very difficult to control. In particular, many lives have been lost in this area. I think that everyone saw television programs which showed the tragedy that has afflicted this part of the African continent. There have been many deaths in Sahel, as well as important losses of cattle, and economic goods.
That disaster has shown how urgent it is to develop systematically water resources to prevent repetition of such a disaster. However, the lack of technical resources and expertise in that area has considerably affected the efforts of the Ethiopian government to lower the level of suffering and
